query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a high-pressure (on the order of several GPa) rapid quenching treatment immediately after melt homogenization will enhance the glass-forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized melt of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy intended for glass formation.
generation.intervention: Rapid quenching performed under a high-pressure environment (e.g., using a high-pressure quench apparatus maintaining pressures of a few GPa) rather than conventional atmospheric melt quenching.
generation.conditions: This effect is expected when the pressure is sufficiently high to significantly reduce free volume and atomic diffusion in the cooling melt; the intervention may not produce the desired effect if pressures are too low or if the cooling rate is not maintained. It is most effective when the alloy composition and initial melt conditions allow for a critical suppression of crystalline nucleation.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased atomic packing density and reduced atomic mobility (diffusivity) during transition from liquid to solid, which suppresses the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
generation.mechanism: Under high pressure, the free volume available in the melt decreases, thereby retarding atomic diffusion and the kinetics of crystalline nucleation. This leads to a lower critical cooling rate required for glass formation and results in an amorphous structure that is more thermally stable against crystallization.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increased crystallization onset temperature and improved stability of the amorphous phase compared to samples processed at atmospheric pressure. In addition, a higher fraction of the material should remain amorphous (with lower evidence of crystallinity) post processing.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed via conventional atmospheric pressure melt quenching, which typically exhibit lower glass-forming ability and reduced thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only if the applied pressure and cooling rate are above threshold values; if the pressure is below approximately 2 GPa or if the cooling rate is not sufficiently high, then the suppression of crystallization may not occur. Very high pressures or extreme conditions might trigger alternative phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in glass-forming ability and the optimal pressure and cooling rate parameters are not yet determined and will require systematic experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the same phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy melt. For Batch A, apply a high-pressure (~2–6 GPa) rapid quenching treatment immediately after homogenization. For Batch B, perform conventional melt quenching at atmospheric pressure under otherwise identical conditions. Characterize both batches using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine crystallization onset temperatures, X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess the amorphous versus crystalline phase fractions, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for microstructural analysis.
measurements: Amorphous fraction and phase analysis via XRD
Microstructure and presence of nuclei via TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-pressure quenched samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in crystallization onset temperature and amorphous phase fraction (i.e., if they are similar or inferior to the atmospheric pressure quenched samples), the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: Can high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in eutectic high entropy alloys (EHEAs) that are typically strong yet brittle?. System: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (Al 14.8 Co 21.3 Cr 21.3 Fe 21.3 Ni 21.3 at. %). Processing: Homogenized alloy subjected to HPHT treatment at 6 GPa and 1473 K for 2 hours using a self-designed hexahedron-anvil-press apparatus. Test conditions: Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹.
